definition.text: Inflation is a rise in the average price of goods and services measured in money, which means each unit of money buys less.

facts.text: It is measured with a price index, usually a consumer price index, and the inflation rate is the yearly percentage change in that index.
Its opposite, a fall in the general price level, is deflation.
Inflation refers to the general trend of prices, not a change in any single price.
Causes include growth in the money supply, demand shocks, supply shocks such as energy crises, interest-rate cuts and changing expectations.
High or unpredictable inflation harms an economy: it makes long-term planning hard and uncertainty about money's future value discourages saving and investment.
It shifts buying power away from people on fixed incomes, such as pensioners whose pensions are not indexed to prices.
Most economists today favour a low and steady inflation rate, a task usually given to central banks.
Since the Great Depression of the 1930s, prices have generally risen every year.

definition.text: Climateflation is inflation driven by climate change, through its effects on food production and supply chains.

facts.text: The term, first used by Isabel Schnabel of the European Central Bank, covers price rises from heat, droughts and floods that hit farm output.
In 2022–2023, climate-driven heat in Europe raised food prices by about 0.7%, adding about 0.3% to overall inflation.
The same study found warming expected by 2035 could raise these effects by 30–50%.
A related term, fossilflation, describes inflation caused by fossil fuel prices, which push up transport, food and shipping costs.

definition.text: Inflation targeting is a monetary policy in which the central bank keeps adjusting its interest rate to steer inflation towards an official target.

facts.text: It began in New Zealand in 1990 and has spread to most developed countries.
In most OECD countries the target is about 2%.
Research suggests true inflation runs about one percentage point below the official figure, so a 2% target keeps true inflation from nearing zero or deflation.

title: Theories of inflation

definition.text: Economists have long debated what causes inflation, with competing theories such as the quantity theory of money and the real bills doctrine.

facts.text: Keynes argued in 1936 that wages and prices are sticky in the short run but respond gradually to swings in demand.
In the 1960s Milton Friedman's monetarism challenged this view, holding that inflation is always and everywhere a monetary phenomenon.
In the 1970s the link between inflation and unemployment broke down, which was eventually put down to changing inflation expectations.
Since about 2000 the common view gives roles to demand shocks, supply shocks and inflation expectations.

contested_note: Rival schools have disputed inflation's causes for centuries, from the quantity theory versus real bills to Keynesians versus monetarists.
